analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' windfall profits when crude prices spike and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill has 27 cosponsors, all Democrats, but has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee with no vote or hearing since it was referred in March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill puts a 50% excise tax on the profits large oil companies make when crude oil prices rise above their 2025 average — in effect, taxing only the windfall from a price spike, not normal profits. The money collected goes into a fund that sends rebates back to individual taxpayers. It applies only to companies that extract or import more than 300,000 barrels a day, and the rebates phase out for households above $75,000 in income ($150,000 for couples).
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers, especially lower- and middle-income households, who would receive gasoline price rebates whenever oil prices surge past the 2025 baseline. Joint filers get 150% of the standard rebate, and the credit is fully refundable, so people who owe little or no income tax still get the money. The rebate phases out only above $75,000 for singles and $150,000 for joint returns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle- and lower-income taxpayers during price spikes

how_it_helps.text: The tax is 50% of the amount by which the average quarterly Brent crude price exceeds its 2025 average, so it only applies to profits that come from a price spike, not to earnings at normal price levels.
All revenue from the tax is appropriated into a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and paid out as quarterly rebates to eligible individuals.
The rebate is a fully refundable tax credit, meaning households that owe little or no income tax still receive the full amount.

Joint filers receive 150% of the standard rebate amount, and the credit phases down by 5% of income over $75,000 ($150,000 for joint returns), concentrating the benefit on households with lower incomes.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies — only those that extracted or imported more than 300,000 barrels of crude per day in 2025, or exceed that rate in a given quarter — pay the excise tax on every barrel. If they pass some of the tax through to gasoline prices, consumers would bear part of the cost, though rebates would offset that for most households.

drawbacks.text: Oil companies could raise gasoline prices to pass the tax through to consumers, partially or fully offsetting the rebate for some households, particularly those whose rebates are phased out at higher incomes but who still buy gas.
The tax and the rebates only kick in when crude prices exceed their 2025 average; if prices stay below that baseline, the program generates no revenue and pays nothing.
Only companies above the 300,000 barrel-per-day threshold pay the tax, so smaller producers are exempt and gain a relative cost advantage over the larger companies the bill targets.
A tax on every barrel produced could discourage drilling in periods of high prices, which would increase supply less than a policy without the tax would.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is targeted: it taxes only price-spike windfalls and returns the money directly to consumers, with the phase-out concentrating the rebate on households that spend the largest share of income on gas. The main honest concern is cost pass-through — if oil companies raise pump prices, some consumers, especially higher-income ones whose rebates shrink to zero, could end up paying more at the pump without a matching rebate. Whether companies can pass the tax through depends on market conditions the bill cannot control.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which controls tax legislation, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on March 17, 2026, joined by Reps. Magaziner and Tlaib as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the required first step for any tax bill.
27 members have cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, large oil companies are better off: the tax has not advanced and no revenue has been collected, while households get no rebates because the bill has not become law.

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all of them Democrats, giving the bill its only demonstrated support.

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; no roll-call votes have occurred yet.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers (300,000+ barrels per day)
industries.note: The bill would tax these companies 50% of the amount by which crude prices exceed their 2025 average, on every barrel extracted in or imported into the United States. Their financial interest in stopping the bill runs against the public's interest in receiving rebates during price spikes.

industries.industry: Smaller oil producers (below the 300,000 barrel-per-day threshold)
industries.note: They are exempt from the tax, which would give them a cost advantage over larger competitors when prices spike. The benefit to consumers from rebates is not tied to them.

analysis.trajectory: A tax bill introduced by a minority-party member with 27 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support faces long odds in the Ways and Means Committee, where the majority controls the schedule. Most such bills die quietly without a hearing. Unless oil prices spike sharply enough to create political pressure or the bill attracts majority-party support, it is likely to remain in committee through the end of the 119th Congress.
